title: Ops telemetry curator and taskified playbook handoff
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Oncall frequently needs curated telemetry and a compact set of runbook fragments relevant to the current incident snapshot. Current handoffs are ad-hoc (Slack threads, links to sprawling runbooks) which increases mean time to resolution and causes repeated context-switching for junior responders.

Goal: Build a lightweight Ops Telemetry Curator service and a Playbook Handoff interface that turns a selected incident snapshot into a small, ranked set of taskified runbook fragments and signal slices. The output should be consumable by the admin CLI and the runbooks-as-tasks executor so responders can launch safe remediation steps with a consistent audit trail.

Scope:
- Curator microservice that accepts incident snapshot (JSON) and returns 3–7 prioritized runbook fragments plus relevant telemetry URIs.
- A thin UI endpoint in the ops console to preview and export a curated task bundle.
- Integrations: admin-cli (for one-click task import), runbook-executor API (to schedule typed tasks), and telemetry links (Grafana panels, traces).
- Audit metadata (who curated, policy version, timestamp) persisted to the incident record for compliance.

Non-goals: full NLP-based runbook generation, replacing the existing runbook catalog, or automating escalations without human sign-off.
acceptance_criteria: Given an incident snapshot the curator returns a ranked list of 3-7 runbook fragments with confidence scores
Ops console preview shows fragments and telemetry links, and an export button creates a task bundle consumable by admin-cli
Exported bundle includes audit metadata and a stable bundle id persisted to the incident record
Runbook fragments link to source canonical runbook and a GitHub PR or edit history where applicable
End-to-end test that imports the bundle via admin-cli into a staging runbook-executor and runs a dry-run without side-effects
design_decisions:
We opted for a rule-first curator with lightweight heuristics (signal templates + fragment match) rather than an ML classifier in phase 1 to keep behavior auditable and easy to iterate. Fragments are small JSON objects (title, steps[], tags[], source_runbook, safety_level) so the runbook-executor can validate inputs and enforce safe-mode gating.

Trade-offs: rule-first means some false positives on novel incidents but lowers risk of unsafe automation. Building a simple confidence score (0-100) will allow PM and SRE to tune thresholds without redeploys.

Rollout: start behind a feature flag for SRE + Oncall alpha group, collect curator suggestions vs. what responders actually used for 4 weeks, then iterate to phase 2 (ML ranking) if we observe >60% acceptance rate.
implementation_notes:
Backend: Go service with a thin HTTP API; reuse existing incident snapshot schema used by infra-alerts. Store bundles in incidents table (postgres) with JSONB for fragment payloads.

Admin-CLI: add `ops export-bundle <bundle-id>` command that writes a taskfile compatible with runbook-executor v2 (see spec in repo).

Runbook fragments: canonicalization script that normalizes fragments across runbook sources; a small linter will run in CI to enforce safety tags.

Telemetry links: produce prefiltered Grafana/Jaeger URLs that include incident trace ids and time windows.

Telemetry: emit curator.suggestions.count and curator.bundle.acceptance with tags {team, incident_severity} to the metrics pipeline.
qa_plan:
1) Unit tests for fragment matcher and confidence heuristics.
2) Integration test that creates synthetic snapshot -> curator returns expected bundle.
3) End-to-end staging run that exports and dry-runs tasks in runbook-executor with feature flag.
4) Manual alpha testing sessions with two SREs and the oncall rotation to validate UX and audit persistence.
open_questions: Should curator be allowed to add parameterized remediation steps (e.g. restart-service) or only link to fragments that require manual fill-in?
What retention period for exported bundles is reasonable for audit vs. DB storage cost (30 vs 90 days)?
Do we need to introduce RBAC on who can export and run bundles, or rely on existing incident permissions?
